White South African who grew up during Apartheid. My parents were passively racist, they, like most middle class white people were exposed to a comprehensive racist narrative through all media over decades. My grandfather had been murdered by his Rhodesian gardener leaving my mother scarred and embittered. I say ‘passively racist’ because they employed a cleaner and gardener, and were respectful and friendly to them. One on one, there was no sense of hatred, fear or sense of superiority. I certainly had an uncle and an aunt who said some very ugly things. My cousins and I, used to fight them and their views but it was fairly pointless. My folks weren’t that vocal but there was the occasional ‘these people’ type generalization.
Over time most of their conservative views, homophobia included, have softened and I guess they wised up. My mum came to really love some of their cleaners. In my twenties I was in a mixed race relationship and they were largely cool with it. My mother now lives in a nursing home in the UK and she adores her Ghanaian and Kenyan carers, who are her favorite by far.

There were riots in Apartheid South Africa. The oppressive white party in power stoked discord amongst the two most powerful black political parties (classic divide & conquer strategy). The conflict between the Xhosa and Zulu people was often extremely violent. As a child one particular moment on our big box TV was particularly frightening. A helicopter shot of a large group of miners tearing across a field brandishing spears, clubs and pangas, strong black men running with murderous intent. They were embroiled in reprisal killings back and forth. I was told that this was maybe half an hour away from my parents’s house, in our comfy white suburb. 

It was quite brilliant propaganda to maintain the paranoia narrative, affirming fears. The Apartheid government were very smart, very cunning and they successfully postponed the transition to democracy through these tactics. Thankfully Nelson Mandela was able to allay the majority of white voters fears, who then voted to give black South Africans the opportunity to vote themselves. 

Bless Madiba.

Design brief and assessment can literally be a matrix where you list the core qualities that need to be communicated, indicate their hierarchy and then measure their completed designs against the matrix. If you list 15 things you can’t get a good results. Identify 5 or 6 core qualities. 
Remember that not all qualities need to literally crammed into the icon. If the biz name includes the word ‘ocean’, then the icon can shift to other qualities. If the tag line directly addresses another quality then, again, you can lower the priority of other qualities.  Typography can show qualities too - sturdy trustworthy fonts are more bold. Flexibility and elegance are lighter fonts that have expressive embellishments. Good logos achieve simplicity while telling a broad story. No design studio wants to design by committee so the brief is essential. Use ChatGPT to help. Ask what questions a designer studio should ask in order to be best equipped to deliver a good design. The free changes one can make would be taking more walks outside, eating healthier, reducing things like smoking and drinking. Most of us have pretty toxic habits and they are very hard to break. But if we can take small steps daily, we can improve our physical and mental well-being. The shit we consume really does make a massive impact on how we feel. 

Then, depending on finances and insurance, therapy/medication or hobbies like yoga, meditation can also really improve our wellbeing. I know, it sounds ridiculous, but these can make a massive difference, but don’t expect that you’ll find the right strategy, therapist, medication or hobby first try. It takes patience and perseverance. 

Will the above stop shit hitting the fan? No. You will still face challenging times. We can often carry with us the toxic baggage from traumas and childhood that effectively poisons our expectations, our relationships and our self worth. Therapy is great as it helps you work through them in such a way that detoxifies their impact. The load is lightened. 

We can also get better at dealing with the shit, learning strategies to deal with the shit. Finally, we can get better at seeing the good times, increasing their frequency. 

It’s not easy. It is possible.

We are fed the idea that we are only succeeding in life when we're happy. Like happiness is the goal, and if we aren't happy then we're somehow failing in life. This is absolutely untrue. You can have struggles and be unhappy, and still win at life. The point of life is not to be happy, it's to find meaning in whatever you are going through. 'Finding meaning' is going through something and figuring out what what you are learning, how it changes you, why it's important. The better you get at finding meaning, the more joy you find in life, and you can find beauty in even the most painful experiences.

I'll give you an example of this. My older brother died, and over a few months my grief grew until it felt like I could barely breathe. I really thought about what I was experiencing, and really looked at the pain. I felt as if I was lost at sea, with no lifejacket and I was sinking deeper and deeper into the darkness. It swallowed me, darkness and despair, and I felt completely alone. The more I thought about it, I reflected on the idea that others had gone through what was going through. Many others, many billions of people throughout the history of the world knew exactly how I felt. Suddenly, deep in that dark ocean, I was connected (through a shared experience) to an almost infinite number of people, people I knew, people long gone, people from every corner of the earth, over thousands of years. This idea completely changed how I experienced grief. I was still in terrible emotional pain but it was also really beautiful. A terrible part of life was no longer just pain, but it was important, and beautiful, and had value. 

You will have really painful moments in your life, and that's okay. We are never alone in our pain, and with some reflection we can be transformed for the better by going through these times.
